title: Trapping the Center: A Journey into Geometric Probability
text:
Imagine you have a circular piece of plywood. You randomly hammer 6 nails into the very edge of the circle. If you wrap a rubber band around those nails, what are the odds that the center of the wood is trapped inside that rubber band?
This is a pretty classic problem in the field of geometric probability. The idea was inspired by a video I saw online, but a detailed write-up can also be found at Brainstellar (along with some other really interesting puzzles!)

title: Trapping the Center: A Journey into Geometric Probability
Trapping the Center: A Journey into Geometric Probability
text:
The Mathematical Derivation
For pretty much all questions even loosely related to probability, it can be insightful to think about the complementary case.
Does this principle apply in this case? Well, trapping the center kind of warrants a sort of “balance” around the circle. However, moving one point slightly may break the trap, or it may not, and reasoning about this delicate interleaving of all n points is going to be quite complex. This is… a very loose justification to say the least, but the fact that success requires some form of coordination, and failure is usually simpler, may help us here.
So instead of calculating the probability of the center being inside, let’s consider the probability of the center being outside.

1. The Crucial Condition
Let’s define what it means for the center to be inside of such a shape. Imagine you are standing at the exact center of the circle. If you are not trapped, there must be an escape route - a straight line you can walk along to infinity without ever bumping into the rubber band.
Visualize walking along this path. Since you never hit a wall, you are effectively “phasing” out of the circle’s interior. Once you are far enough out, you can look back and see that the entire group of nails is situated on the opposite side of the circle from your path. This is the crucial condition!


2. Math Time!
To help us simplify the calculations, let us make another important observation.
For all points to lie in one semicircle, there must exist a gap between adjacent points larger than 180°
The circle is \(360^\circ\), so it’s impossible to have two gaps larger than \(180^\circ\), thus there is exactly one specific gap that we will call the “Big Gap”.
Since this gap is unique, we can simply sum the probabilities of the gap starting at each point. To do this, let’s pick a specific point, \(P_1\). What are the odds that the gap immediately following \(P_1\) is larger than \(180^\circ\)? This means all other \(n-1\) points have to be somewhere in the other \(180^\circ\) of the circle. Each point separately has a \(1/2\) chance to land there, giving us \(\left( 1/2 \right) ^{n-1}\) for \(n-1\) overall.
Now, since any of these \(n\) points could start the “Big Gap” (and, importantly, that these events are all mutually exclusive), we sum them up:
\[
P(Outside)
= n \times \left( \frac{1}{2} \right) ^{n-1}
= \frac{n}{2^{n-1}}
\]
and DON’T FORGET THIS IS THE COMPLEMENT, so the probability the center is inside the shape is the complement, or
\[
P(Inside)
= 1-P(Outside)
= 1-\frac{n}{2^{n-1}}
\]

Follow-Ups
Among the more astute readers may have noticed a striking connection with the 3Blue1Brown video, “The Hardest Problem on the Hardest Test”. This is not a coincidence, and it is infact a 3D version of basically the exact same problem. Instead of a circle, they use a sphere, and instead of a semicircle, the problem deals with a hemisphere.
Here are some follow-up questions you can try:

If you pick 3 random points on a circle, what is the probability that the triangle they form is obtuse?
(Hard) If you pick 4 random points in a convex region (like a circle), what is the probability that one point lies inside the triangle formed by the others?
